text: A Google Doodle is a temporary, special alteration of the Google homepage logo used to commemorate holidays, events, achievements, and historical figures. The first Doodle, created in 1998 to mark the Burning Man event in Black Rock City, Nevada, was designed by co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin to inform users of their absence in case the servers crashed. Early Doodles were managed by marketing employee Susan Wojcicki, who led initiatives such as an alien landing and holiday-themed logos. From 1998 to 2000, Doodles were designed by cartoonist Ian David Marsden, after which Page and Brin asked public relations officer Dennis Hwang to design a Bastille Day logo, marking the beginning of an internal team known as the Doodlers, who now organize and publish Doodles. Initially static and non-hyperlinked, Doodles evolved by the 2010s: on October 31, 2000, the first animated Doodle celebrated Halloween, and on May 21, 2010, the first interactive Doodle, a playable Pac-Man created in association with Namco, debuted, featuring the Google letters in a maze and mimicking the original arcade game’s sounds. The "Insert Coin" button allowed one or two players to play, with a third press triggering an "I'm Feeling Lucky" search. The Doodle was removed on May 23, 2010, but a permanent site to play it was later released due to high user demand, with an estimated 1 billion players worldwide. By 2014, Google had published over 2,000 regional and international Doodles, often featuring guest artists, musicians, and personalities, and by 2024, the Doodlers had created over 5,000 Doodles globally. Doodles honor artists, scientists, and historical events, such as the 50th anniversary of the Lego brick, and are used to mark Google’s own milestones. Some Doodles are country-specific, while others appear worldwide. Since the first Thanksgiving Doodle in 1998, many annual Doodles for holidays and events have been recurring. The Doodlers team includes illustrators, engineers, and artists such as Ekua Holmes, Sophia Foster-Dimino, Lynnette Haozous, and Eric Carle. Google also runs Doodle 4 Google, a student competition that began in the UK, expanded to the US and other countries, and included events in Ireland (2008), India (2009), and Singapore (2010 and 2015), with winning designs displayed on national homepages. In 2007, Google faced criticism for posting a Roald Dahl Doodle on the day of Rosh Hashanah, leading to its immediate removal with no record in the official archive. In the same year, Google featured a Veterans Day Doodle despite criticism for omitting other patriotic holidays. In 2014, Google faced backlash for not honoring the 70th anniversary of D-Day, instead featuring Japanese Go player Honinbo Shusaku, prompting the company to remove the logo and add links to D-Day images. In 2016, a Doodle honoring Yuri Kochiyama, an activist with controversial views, drew criticism from conservative commentators and Senator Pat Toomey, who called for an apology, though Google did not respond or alter the Doodle. A 2014 SPARK Movement report highlighted a gender and racial imbalance in Doodles, with most honoring white males, prompting Google to commit to increasing representation of women and racial minorities. Google officially states in its guidelines that it does not create Doodles for religious holidays, avoiding religious themes or iconography, though it recognizes non-religious celebrations derived from religious holidays such as Valentine’s Day, Holi, and Tu B'Av. Critics argue that Google inconsistently applies this policy, noting the absence of Doodles for major Christian holidays like Easter and Christmas, despite celebrating Holi and Tu B'Av. While Christmas is not explicitly named, a seasonal Doodle has appeared on December 25 since 1999, and since the mid-2010s, a similar Doodle has been shown on January 7 (Eastern Orthodox Christmas) without using the term "Christmas" or "Eastern Orthodox Church." Google first created an Easter Doodle in 2000 and only returned to it in 2019 with a desktop-only, atypical Doodle where the Google logo remained unchanged and clicking the "I'm Feeling Lucky" button triggered an Easter-themed animation with linked items; this entry was later removed from the official archive. The 2019 Doodle was not visible on mobile devices unless "Desktop mode" was enabled, and Google’s technologist Danny Sullivan explained it was difficult to make the interactivity work reliably on mobile. In 2020, Google celebrated Easter again with a non-Doodle Easter egg below the search buttons, with hovertext "Happy Easter" and a link to a search results page, similar to how it has recognized Memorial Day and Remembrance Day in the US.
